contentHtml:
What payment gateway integration involves

In short: For most Indian apps and websites, the choice is between Razorpay, PayU, Cashfree and PhonePe PG, whose standard plans list roughly 1.95% to 2% per domestic payment plus GST, with launch offers that cut this to zero for a while. Stripe is invite-only for Indian businesses. The harder part is the integration: verifying payments on your server, handling webhooks, refunds and settlement, and following RBI's rules for recurring payments and saved cards.

I read each gateway's own pricing page and developer docs, and the RBI directions that apply, and kept only what they say. Where two pages from the same company disagree, I say so, because that is exactly the kind of thing that surprises a business after launch.

This guide was checked in November 2026. Gateway pricing pages change often and most of them are running offers right now, so read the current page and the offer terms before you sign.

Gateway pricing compared

These are the standard, published rates for a small or mid business. Enterprise and high-volume businesses are offered custom pricing by all of them.

Published standard rates for domestic online payments, November 2026

GatewayStandard domestic rateHigher-rate methodsOffer on the pageSetup or annual fee
Razorpay2% + GSTSome methods priced separately on the page0% for the first 90 days ("down from 2%")None
PayU2% (cards, net banking, wallets, BNPL), GST extra3% for EMI, Amex, Diners and internationalNone shownNone
CashfreeFrom 1.95% platform fee, excl. GSTInternational cards 2.99%, Amex 2.95%0% on first ₹20 lakh GMV for new merchants, till 31 March 2027None
PhonePe PG1.99% standard planNot listed by method on the page I read"Super Savings Offer", free with T&CNone
Stripe India2% for Indian Visa and Mastercard3% for cards issued outside IndiaNone shownInvite-only in India

Source: Razorpay pricing and PayU pricing and Cashfree pricing and PhonePe PG pricing and Stripe India pricing, read 16 November 2026.

Stripe's support page says businesses from India cannot sign up for a new account through its website and must request an invite. If you are building for Indian customers, plan around one of the Indian gateways unless Stripe has already invited you.

PhonePe's page notes that PhonePe Limited is an RBI authorised Payment Aggregator. Whichever gateway you choose, I would check the same thing: that it is authorised by RBI as a payment aggregator, because RBI's e-mandate directions, for one, make the acquirer responsible for its merchants' compliance.

What the headline rate hides

Zero MDR on UPI is not zero fees

You will read that UPI is free for merchants. Razorpay's pricing FAQ explains the catch clearly: there is zero MDR (Merchant Discount Rate) on standard bank-to-bank UPI, so the bank does not charge you, but a platform or technology fee of 2% still applies for the gateway's dashboard, reporting and infrastructure. Razorpay says the same zero MDR applies to RuPay debit cards. PayU's page says UPI P2P has zero MDR and merchant UPI pricing varies by business type and volume. Cashfree says its UPI charges are "as per the applicable law".

So ask each gateway one direct question: what will I pay, in rupees, on a ₹1,000 UPI payment? Get the answer in writing.

Offers end

Razorpay's 0% applies for the first 90 days. Cashfree's festive offer covers new merchants on their first ₹20 lakh of GMV, until 31 March 2027, and the terms say it ends when you use it up, when the campaign ends, or on a fair-usage disqualification. PhonePe marks its offer with T&C. Budget at the standard rate from day one and treat the offer as a bonus.

GST is on top

Razorpay quotes 2% + GST and says the fee and GST are deducted from each payment before settlement. PayU says GST is extra, and Cashfree's prices exclude GST. Your bank receives the payment minus fee minus GST on the fee, which is what your accounts team needs to reconcile.

Settlement times: when the money reaches your bank

Settlement is when the gateway pays captured money into your bank account. T is the day of capture, so T+2 means two working days later. Working days exclude bank holidays.

Razorpay's settlements documentation says the standard cycle for domestic payments is T+2 working days, and gives a T+7 example for international payments, which may also have part held as a reserve. Its pricing FAQ says money is settled "typically T+1 or Instant". Those two pages do not match, so ask for your settlement cycle in your agreement. Razorpay also says the cycle is subject to bank approval and can vary with your business vertical and risk.

PayU's pricing page says standard settlement is T+2, with same-day and priority settlement available for some business categories, sometimes for a fee. Cashfree's offer terms give T+1 settlement by 8:00 PM IST as the default during the campaign. Razorpay, PayU and Cashfree all price faster settlement separately.

KYC: what you need before you can go live

Gateways will let you test in sandbox mode straight away, but live payments wait for KYC. The documents depend on your business type. Razorpay's list is typical of what I would expect elsewhere:

  • Individual or unregistered business: PAN, address proof (fetched from CKYC where possible) and bank account details.
  • Proprietorship: two proofs of business, chosen from MSME/Udyam, GST, Shop & Establishment, Import Export Code or a postpaid mobile bill, plus the owner's PAN, address proof and bank details.
  • Private or public limited company: certificate of incorporation, MOA and AOA, business PAN, bank details, the authorised signatory's PAN and address proof, a board resolution or power of attorney, and a declaration of beneficial owners with more than 10% shareholding.

Razorpay says the PAN and the signatory's address proof must belong to the same person, and if bank verification fails it asks for a video of a cancelled cheque. The common delay is a mismatch: the bank account name, PAN name and business name must line up. Fix that before you apply, not after.

I would also have the website ready before applying: clear pricing, contact details, terms, a privacy policy and a refund policy.

RBI rules for UPI AutoPay, recurring payments and saved cards

E-mandates and UPI AutoPay

RBI's Digital Payments, E-mandate Framework, 2026, dated 21 April 2026, consolidates the rules for recurring payments on cards, prepaid instruments and UPI. This is what applies to subscriptions, monthly fees and UPI AutoPay:

  • Registration needs an additional factor of authentication (AFA), and so does the first transaction. They can be combined if the first payment happens at registration.
  • Every mandate has a validity period, and the customer can modify or withdraw it at any time.
  • The issuer sends a pre-transaction notification at least 24 hours before each debit, with the merchant name, amount, date and reason, and the customer can opt out of that debit.
  • Recurring transactions up to ₹15,000 each can go through without AFA. Above that, AFA is needed every time.
  • Insurance premiums, mutual fund subscriptions and credit card bill payments can go without AFA up to ₹1,00,000 per transaction.
  • No charges may be levied on the customer for using e-mandates, and the acquirer must ensure its merchants comply.

For your product, that means two things. A monthly plan above ₹15,000 will ask the customer to authenticate every month, so expect some payments to fail when they do not. And because customers get notified and can opt out, your app has to handle a skipped debit without cutting off a paying customer by mistake.

Card tokenisation

Since 1 October 2022, merchants cannot store the clear card number, CVV, expiry date or other sensitive card data for online payments, as SBI's customer FAQ on RBI's card-on-file tokenisation explains. Saved cards now work through tokens: a 16-digit number unique to the card, the token requestor and the merchant. Customers choose whether to tokenise, and SBI says they pay nothing for it.

In practice, never build your own "save card" table. Use the gateway's saved-card or token feature, and keep card fields inside the gateway's checkout so card data never touches your server.

Webhooks and reconciliation

A payment can succeed after your customer has closed the app. The phone loses network, the bank responds late, or the customer switches to a UPI app and never comes back. Webhooks are how the gateway tells your server what really happened.

Razorpay's webhook best practices are specific, and I would design any integration to the same standard:

  • Respond with a 2xx status within 5 seconds. Razorpay treats anything else, including a slow response, as a failed delivery and sends the event again.
  • Failed deliveries are retried with exponential backoff for 24 hours after the event was created.
  • Delivery is at least once, so the same event can arrive more than once. Use the x-razorpay-event-id header to ignore duplicates.
  • Events may arrive out of order.
  • Verify the webhook signature so you only trust events that really came from the gateway.
  • For business-critical cases, Razorpay suggests also polling its payment APIs, since webhooks are asynchronous.

Reconciliation is the daily check that three numbers agree: orders marked paid in your system, payments captured in the gateway dashboard, and money settled into your bank. If you only do one thing from this post, do this. We wrote more on the engineering side in webhooks you can rely on.

Refunds and failed payments

Razorpay offers normal refunds, which reach the customer in 5 to 7 working days, and instant refunds, which arrive almost immediately. There is a second kind of refund many teams do not plan for. A payment can sit in an "authorized" state, where the customer's money is blocked but the merchant has not captured it. Razorpay's capture settings say authorized payments that are not captured within the timeout, 3 days by default, are refunded automatically. If your order system waits for a capture that never comes, the customer is refunded and you ship nothing, or worse, ship anyway.

RBI's 2019 circular on turnaround times also sets limits for failed payments. For UPI, where the customer's account is debited but the merchant does not get confirmation, the amount must be auto-reversed within T+5 days, with ₹100 per day of compensation for any delay beyond that. Your support team should know it.

Step by step: integrating a gateway properly

Step 1. Decide what you are charging for. One-time payments, subscriptions, split payments to vendors or refunds at scale each need different products from the gateway. If your app sells digital content, check the app store rules first; our post on app store rejections covers when Apple and Google require their own billing.

Step 2. Start KYC on day one. Put the website pages up and submit documents while development starts in sandbox mode.

Step 3. Create the order on your server. The amount comes from your database, never from the app or browser. The customer's device can be tampered with.

Step 4. Use the gateway's hosted checkout or SDK. Card details stay inside the gateway's screens, which keeps you out of card storage and tokenisation rules.

Step 5. Verify on the server. When checkout returns, check the payment signature and the payment status through the gateway's API before you mark the order paid.

Step 6. Add webhooks. Handle payment captured, failed and refunded events, respond within the gateway's time limit, and make every handler safe to run twice.

Step 7. Set capture rules. Auto-capture unless you have a reason not to, and alert someone about payments stuck in authorized.

Step 8. Test the bad paths. Closed app mid-payment, UPI app timeout, double tap on Pay, refund of a partly refunded order, a webhook arriving before the browser redirect. Then reconcile a test day end to end.

Three worked examples

These are illustrative businesses, not clients. The numbers are invented to show how the rules apply.

A clinic taking consultation fees

A clinic charges ₹500 per online consultation and patients mostly pay by UPI. At a 2% platform fee, each payment costs about ₹10 plus GST on that fee, even though UPI itself has zero MDR. The main risk is refunds: cancelled appointments need a clear refund policy on the site and a quick way for the receptionist to refund from the dashboard. If the doctor calls a patient whose payment is stuck as authorized, the team should know it will auto-refund rather than promise a manual refund on top.

A D2C brand with prepaid orders

A clothing brand gets prepaid orders on its website and app. The danger is marking orders paid from the browser redirect. A customer closes the tab during a UPI payment, the payment succeeds a minute later, and the order sits as "pending" while the customer is charged. The fix is to fulfil only on a verified webhook, and to run a daily reconciliation of paid orders against captured payments and settlements. Our post on checkout conversion covers the customer-facing side.

A coaching institute with monthly fees

An institute wants to collect a ₹4,000 monthly fee through UPI AutoPay or card e-mandates. That is under RBI's ₹15,000 limit, so after the first authenticated payment, later debits can go through without AFA. Each student's parent will get a notice at least 24 hours before each debit and can opt out, so the institute's system must expect some months to fail and send a payment link instead of locking the student out. If it later moves to a ₹20,000 quarterly fee, every debit would need AFA.

Common integration mistakes

Trusting the client. Taking the amount or the success status from the app or browser. Both can be faked. The server decides the amount and checks the status.

No idempotency. Webhooks arrive more than once. Without a check on the event or payment ID, one payment can create two orders or two wallet credits.

Slow webhook handlers. Sending emails or generating invoices inside the webhook means you miss the 5-second response window on Razorpay, the gateway retries, and you do the work again. Acknowledge first, process in the background.

Ignoring authorized payments. They auto-refund after the capture timeout, which confuses customers and support alike.

Storing card data. Even the last four digits plus expiry in your own table is asking for trouble. Use the gateway's tokens.

Live keys in the app. Secret API keys belong only on your server. The app and website get only the public key.

Choosing on the offer. A 0% offer for 90 days matters less than settlement time, support quality and whether the gateway supports the payment products you need next year.

If you would rather have this built once and correctly, our team does ecommerce development and payment integrations with the gateway account, code and cloud kept in the client's name. A daily and monthly reconciliation routine

A reconciliation routine for a small business

WhenWhat to checkWhat a problem looks like
Daily, 10 minutesOrders marked paid vs payments captured in the dashboardA captured payment with no paid order, or the reverse
DailyPayments stuck in authorizedAny older than a day, before the auto-refund
On each settlementSettlement amount vs captured payments minus fees and GSTA shortfall you cannot explain
WeeklyRefunds issued vs refunds requestedA refund promised but not processed
MonthlyEffective fee rate: total fees divided by total collectedHigher than your standard rate, or an offer that has ended

Source: Razorpay settlements docs and Razorpay capture settings and Razorpay refunds docs, read 16 November 2026.

Keep one spreadsheet or one dashboard view for this. After a month, the effective fee rate tells you whether to ask for better pricing.
